transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Claire Moss (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (Helios ML Platform Lead), Ethan Brooks (Helios SRE), Daniel Kwan (Helios CTO), Marta Lopez (Helios Data Eng)

Summary:
- Deep dive on function/tool-calling and JSON-mode constrained decoding overhead; focus on where latency tax appears and how KV cache + batching + quantization mitigates it for Helios' pipelines.
- Agreed to run shared microbench with Helios prompt set and measure prefix cache hit, p50/p95/token latencies for tool call vs plain generate.
- Follow ups: sample corpus, benchmark configs, pricing pass and pilot kickoff.

Shared artifacts referenced: Shared benchmark sheet: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/helios-kv-batch.xlsx, Draft config snippet: https://redwood.example.com/snippets/constrained-decode.conf

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samira (Redwood AE): yep, good afternoon everyone thanks for carving out time, uh quick round of intros then we'll hand to Diego for the perf bit.
[00:12] Priya (Helios): hi all, Priya here, thanks. we're especially worried about latency when we call external tools from the model — the structured JSON outputs.
[00:21] Diego (Redwood SE): cool, yeah i'll start with an overview then show a couple of traces. high level: function calling adds two overhead vectors — tokenization/parse and constrained decode search space — and then there's the ork of applying schema constraints which can cause extra decode steps.
[00:38] Ethan (Helios SRE): when you say extra decode steps do you mean more tokens generated or more internal beam attempts?
[00:44] Diego: a mix; constrained decoding often means rejecting partial candidates which forces the decoder to explore alternatives, so per-token work rises and tail latency widens. we mitigate via prefix enforcement and token-level pruning.
[00:58] [01:00] Claire (Redwood SE): also KV cache interplay matters: if you have high prefix reuse the KV cache saves almost all early compute, so the marginal overhead of constrained constraints sits on the shorter tail of remaining tokens. if cache misses are high you feel the tax more.
[01:18] Daniel (Helios CTO): our workload has long prompt prefixes (context windows 6k-18k) with a lot of shared system prompts and tool scaffolding, so prefix reuse should be good in theory. question is how bursty user queries are.
[01:33] Marta (Helios): and we often call out to a reranker tool and a taxonomy normalizer which both expect strict JSON — we've seen cases where model glyphs break the schema and we pay to clean up.
[01:45] Diego: right, so two axes to optimize: 1) reduce constrained-search by using scaffold templates that reduce ambiguity, 2) make KV cache effective with smart routing and pinning.
[01:57] [02:00] Samira: quick practical example — we ran a benchmark for a customer with a 4-step tool chain and saw constrained JSON-mode add ~15-35% p95 latency depending on quantization and batch size. we'll share the trace.
[02:15] Priya: can you expand on how quantization interacts? we intend to run on lower-bit elicitation to save cost.
[02:22] Diego: quantization reduces per-token compute but sometimes increases token variability which leads to more re-rolls in constrained decode; the net effect often depends on model family and the decoder kernel. for some LLaMA-family variants, 4-bit optimized kernels had slightly higher p50 but similar p95 when kv hits are high.
[02:40] Ethan: so practically, if we enable 4-bit and rely on KV cache it might be fine?
[02:45] Diego: exactly — KV cache hit rate is the lever. caching prefixes for common system+tool scaffolds avoids decoding those tokens under quantized kernels entirely.
[02:55] [03:00] Priya: what's the recommended cache TTL and shard strategy for a multi-tenant VPC deployment?
[03:07] Claire: TTL depends on churn — for stable system prompts we set effectively infinite TTL and pin them to warm workers. for user-specific data we pick a sliding window 10-60 minutes. shards: route by tenant then by model-version so warm workers serve the pinned prefixes.
[03:22] Daniel: in our private deployment we'll likely have dedicated pools for high-tier customers; does Redwood support pinning across Dedicated and Private?
[03:29] Samira: yes, dedicated pools can pin model variants and prefix caches, and in Private we expose the same control plane APIs so you can configure pins and autoscale rules.
[03:40] [04:00] Diego: i'll show a trace from our microbench: first trace is unconstrained generative baseline, second trace is JSON-mode with schema validation post-decode, third is constrained-decode where we apply token-level masks.
[04:12] Diego: baseline p95 220ms per token; JSON post-validate p95 270ms (extra parse/validate); constrained-decode p95 310ms — but when we applied prefix pinning (kv hit ~82%) constrained p95 fell to 235ms.
[04:34] Priya: those numbers are helpful. what's the batch size?
[04:37] Diego: batch size 8 in that run, on an A100-class GPU with Redwood runtime kernels. we also tested batch 1 for low-latency SLO and saw constrained overhead proportionally larger.
[04:48] [05:00] Ethan: our SLOs are p95 < 300ms for interactive tools; seems borderline in worst case unless we tune.
[05:06] Claire: one lever is dynamic fallback: attempt constrained decode for first N tokens with a soft budget, if exceeded fallback to post-validate; that keeps tail latency bounded while maintaining schema accuracy most of the time.
[05:20] Daniel: any accuracy tradeoffs with fallback? we might accept occasional post-validate fixes if that means staying under SLO.
[05:27] Diego: yes, small tradeoffs — fallback introduces a small number of post-hoc corrections which we can block at pipeline stage for critical outputs. we can also implement hybrid: try constrained decode only for the JSON block, not the whole reply.
[05:41] [06:00] Priya: how do we measure prefix hit rate in our system? do you need logs from our side?
[06:06] Diego: we need sample prompts and the traces; Redwood's agent can run a dry-run and produce a per-request KV hit report and token-level timings. we'll need the Helios prompt set.
[06:18] Samira: action item: Priya to send the 100-sample prompt set.
[06:21] Priya: will do.
[06:23] [07:00] Diego: quick note on batching: batching improves throughput and amortizes overheads but will increase tail latency for single user requests unless you have async queuing. Redwood supports continuous batching with per-tenant isolation so you can set max latency budget and batch window.
[07:39] Ethan: so for interactive flows we should target batch size 1-2 with micro-batching to minimize latency?
[07:44] Claire: yes, and for background reranks you can run large batches to save cost.
[07:49] Marta: curious about VPC/on-prem specifics: our security team wants to know whether logs from constrained decode (token traces) ever leave our VPC.
[07:59] Samira: in Private mode logs remain in your environment; we ship an agent that collects metrics to your observability pipeline. for Hosted/Dedicated Redwood can push metrics to your SSO-secured console but we don't persist raw prompt content unless opted-in.
[08:13] Daniel: good. what about KMS/HSM for model keys?
[08:16] Claire: we integrate with customer KMS for model encryption and provide options for HSM-backed signing for audit.
[08:22] [08:30] Diego: back to constrained decode overhead — there's also runtime kernel selection: some kernels do faster token sampling under masks; picking the right kernel for the quantized model can materially change p95. we'll include kernel mapping in the bench results.
[08:40] Priya: do you recommend a particular quant/ops combo for large models in our range? (we've toyed with 7B and 13B variants)
[08:47] Diego: for 7B we often recommend 4-bit with optimized kernels; for 13B we test both q4_0 and q4_k variants — the latter sometimes keeps decode variability lower; we'll include those comparison rows.
[08:59] [09:00] Priya: one operational question — if a constrained decode repeatedly fails on a sample, what's the signal we get? is there an auto-fallback?
[09:06] Diego: Redwood runtime emits a constrained-decode status per request: success, soft-fallback, hard-fallback. you can configure auto-fallback thresholds per route.
[09:14] Ethan: sounds useful. can those statuses be exported to our tracing backend?
[09:18] Claire: yes, we have tracing hooks and tag the spans with constrained decode metadata, KV hit, batch id.
[09:25] [10:00] Samira: we wanted to surface an approach for Helios pilot so you can see practical numbers: 1) dry-run microbench on your sample prompts, 2) 1-week pilot on Dedicated pool with pinned prefixes, 3) scale to Private if needed.
[10:39] Daniel: timeline looks okay. what's the expected cost delta for switching from hosted to dedicated for our projected throughput?
[10:46] Samira: we'll send a pricing pass but rough back-of-envelope for your QPS and token mix was 18-25% cheaper on Dedicated when pinning and quantizing aggressively; we'll confirm after microbench.
[10:58] [11:00] Diego: i want to call out a small gotcha — some third-party tool chains do strict JSON with pinned enums; those often cause constrained decode to iterate because of tokenization edge-cases (spaces, punctuation). we recommend normalizing tool contracts to include canonical tokenization hints (e.g., explicit token-sep markers).
[11:23] Priya: is there tooling to generate those canonical hints?
[11:26] Diego: yes, we have a prompt-scaffold generator that inserts token-aware markers; we'll include an example in the benchmark artifacts.
[11:36] [12:00] Marta: for our private deployment, can we run the benchmark on-prem and just share aggregated metrics?
[12:42] Claire: yes that's fine; we can provide a local runner you execute and it uploads aggregated stats. no raw prompts need to leave your network.
[12:53] [13:00] Diego: final thing — batching + KV cache + quantization are orthogonal levers. in our experience the best outcomes come from: pin stable scaffolds, run microbench to pick quant/kernel combos, adopt soft-fallbacks for tight SLOs.
[13:20] Priya: good. please include concrete config snippets.
[13:23] Diego: will do.
[13:28] [14:00] Samira: recap and next steps: we run the microbench, Helios shares prompt corpus, Redwood shares pricing and config snippets, schedule followup week of 7/28.
[14:38] Daniel: thanks everyone.
[14:41] Priya: thanks.
[14:44] [15:00] End of meeting.
